cur:catacombs-lyon-genzano-christ-apostl.summary: Twisted columns and alternating gables and arches form a row of niches, each holding a bearded apostle, with Christ at the centre. Although damaged at the ends, the front preserves the solemn rhythm of a Theodosian columnar sarcophagus.
facts: Commons records that the front came from Genzano near Rome and is in the Musée des Beaux-Arts of Lyon (1937-52).

cur:catacombs2-narbonne-orante-tree-sarc.summary: Trees with interlacing branches divide this sarcophagus into compartments in which biblical figures stand out in high relief. A veiled orant, the praying soul of the deceased, stands at the centre; around her, figures in tunics and togas carry out a series of miracles, including a youthful figure laying his hand on a small child and another pointing his rod, the usual attributes of Christ the wonder-worker. At the right Daniel stands naked between his lions.
facts: The museum label recorded on Commons states that it was found in Narbonne, on the Boulevard de 1848.
Tree sarcophagi, in which trees replace columns as dividers, are a characteristic Western type of the second half of the 4th century; the Louvre and Arles each hold another.
cur:catacombs2-narbonne-orante-tree-sarc.notes: The individual miracle scenes are not identified in the sources consulted; Christ's presence is inferred from the standard iconography (wonder-worker's rod, healing gesture).

cur:monumental-abdallah-nirqi-theophany.summary: Christ, bearded and frontal, appears in a circular glory set within a cloud-like aureole of red and yellow lobes, from which the heads of the living creatures or angels emerge; below at the left stands a smaller figure of a bishop. The bold red outlines and stylised clouds are typical of Nubian painting of the Makurian kingdom.
facts: The Commons source describes the painting as showing a theophany together with a bishop, from the church at Abdallah Nirqi in Nubia.
cur:monumental-abdallah-nirqi-theophany.notes: Current holding institution not confirmed; the image was sourced from UNESCO's 'Museum for Dialogue' website.

vam:O111551.summary: On a cross covered with gold sheets and filigree, a figure of Christ carved from walrus ivory hangs with arms outstretched, crowned and haloed, his head inclined towards his right shoulder and his long hair falling in plaits, wearing an elaborately pleated loincloth. Enamel medallions with the symbols of the four Evangelists mark the arms, and an enamelled titulus above names him IHS NAZARENUS. Behind the figure lay a hollow for relics: the cross is one of the rare survivals of the splendid church treasures of Anglo-Saxon England.
facts: When the ivory figure was removed in 1926 to be photographed and cast, a dried human finger was found in a hollow cut into the wood beneath it.
A fragmentary inscription around the edge of the cross seems to list the relics it once contained; the back shows the Lamb of God and the Evangelist symbols in repoussé gold.

The enamels are unique in Anglo-Saxon art and may have been made by an English goldsmith familiar with German work; the ivory figure resembles late 10th-century manuscripts such as the Ramsey Psalter (V&A).
vam:O111551.notes: The V&A describes it as Anglo-Saxon (probably Winchester), late 10th century, set on an Ottonian cross. The V&A's two texts disagree on whether the finger relic was male or female, so this is not stated. Ex Soltikoff (sale 1861) and Webb collections.
